We already had these things. We could have done all these things at any time in our history. Civilization is a device meant to gaslight or fool people into believing that a hierarchy is legitimate when it is not. It is designed to make people think this hierarchical system is divinely ordained. So, that's the argument I will make today. Before I continue, are you clear about this framework? This is the traditional framework; this is what you've been taught in school. The problem with this framework is that it assumes we're all stupid. And if we're all stupid, how do we explain cave paintings, building kabe, or ko? It assumes all these things.

This new understanding is that we're all capable of creativity but eventually, due to social development, large cities emerge, and the people in charge need to create civilization to justify the hierarchy. So, having said that, let's look at the four earliest major civilizations: Egypt, Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq), the Indus Valley civilization (also called Harappan), and China.

These four have three unique characteristics. First, their latitude is similar; they're not too hot or cold, making them perfect for agriculture. Second, they are located by major rivers—Egypt by the Nile, Mesopotamia by the Tigris and Euphrates, the Indus Valley by the Indus River, and China by the Yellow River. These locations allow for large cities to be built, solving water, transportation, and agricultural problems.

The most important characteristic is that they are near the sea or ocean, enabling trade, bringing in new goods, people, and ideas. Egypt has the Mediterranean and Red Sea; Mesopotamia reaches into the Arabian Sea, connecting to the Indian Ocean; India connects similarly through the urban sea; and China accesses the Pacific.

Over time, because of their trade locations, these civilizations build very large cities. As larger cities grow, they develop colonies upstream and downstream of rivers. This expansion leads to more colonies, forming the basis of civilization with a major city at the center for trade. These areas connect the entire world: Egypt links Europe, the Levant, and Africa; Mesopotamia connects Anatolia, Asia, Central Asia; India similarly; and China, despite the Himalayas, engages in limited but significant trade.

As larger cities expand, they develop colonies to enhance trade reach. This interconnectedness forms the foundation for what we collectively call western civilization. Western civilization isn't just Europe and America; these places have always been in contact with each other, building a shared historical base.
